extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of mathematics; advanced students and researchers in history and philosophy of science/mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Survey and philosophical/historical analysis of the notion of 'style' in mathematics across contexts (national, local, methodological, cognitive), including taxonomies, examples, and epistemological implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style as a category for comparative cultural histories
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'style' to classify cultural patterns and to draw parallels between mathematics and other arts or cultural productions (Spengler, Bense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Spengler's claim that mathematical styles depend on culture and epochs, and Bense's view that style = (aesthetic) form; caution advised because such parallels can be far-fetched and need closer relation to mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: National styles in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to distinctive features of mathematical production that appear to run along national lines (e.g., French vs German styles; 'Deutsche Mathematik').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Duhem, Mehrtens, Bieberbach) show uses and abuses of the category; modern historians treat national styles more cautiously and focus on local cultures or traditions rather than racialized claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local styles (schools, research groups, traditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Styles anchored in local groups, schools, or traditions (research groups, national-institutional cultures) that shape practices, techniques, and transmission of know-how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in historiography to explain how local technical/theoretical know-how affects transferability of practices; contrasted with broader methodological styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological styles (Crombie/Hacking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Styles that are essentially methods of inquiry (e.g., axiomatic postulation, experimental exploration), often listed as distinct scientific styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crombie enumerates several such methods; Hacking and others discuss methodological styles separately from local ones. These may sometimes be interchangeable with 'method'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic (descriptive) vs causal (explanatory) approaches to style
rubrics_metrics.description: Two theorizing modes: (1) descriptive/taxonomic — cataloguing patterns and parallels; (2) causal/explanatory — seeking sociological or psychological causes for the presence of a style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spengler and Bense mix parallels and causes; historians may adopt one or both approaches depending on goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive styles (individual psychological styles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual-level psychological preferences in learning, understanding, or thinking about mathematics (e.g., visual vs analytic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Area of cognitive psychology and math education (Riding, Sternberg & Grigorenko); relevant for explaining intra-individual differences rather than community-level styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic style
rubrics_metrics.description: A style characterized by the axiomatization of theories, defining domains by axioms and seeking minimal, necessary assumptions for results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chevalley and others emphasize how axiomatization changed mathematical writing: demand to identify indispensable properties, provide minimal demonstrations, and delimit domains; examples include Hilbert, Steinitz, Frechet, Lebesgue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epsilon (Weierstrassian) style
rubrics_metrics.description: A style centered on Weierstrassian rigor: intensive use of ε-notation, emphasis on inequalities, arithmetization and careful definitions of limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by heavy use of ε's and a move from equality to inequalities; motivated by the need to rigorize calculus and analysis in the 19th century; Chevalley analyzes its external appearance in writings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive (arithmetization) style
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive approaches that build mathematics from concrete constructions (e.g., constructing complex numbers as pairs of reals) and arithmetization of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chevalley contrasts this with axiomatic approaches; constructive methods sometimes led to artificiality and were supplanted in parts by axiomatization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal style
rubrics_metrics.description: A style emphasizing formal manipulation and symbolic/formal structures (listed among de Lorenzo's styles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in taxonomies of styles; relates to concerns about formalism and its influence on mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric style
rubrics_metrics.description: A style privileging geometric intuition, constructions, and modes of demonstration (listed by de Lorenzo and elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often contrasted with algebraic or analytic styles; historical examples include classical geometry and geometrical approaches to problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic style
rubrics_metrics.description: One of de Lorenzo's named styles; denotes a more literary or rhetorically ornamented mathematical expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Lorenzo lists it among many historical styles but does not fully analyze it; signals role of language in style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cossic style
rubrics_metrics.description: A historical style named by de Lorenzo ('cossic' — referring to algebraic notation/traditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed in de Lorenzo's taxonomy; included for historical taxonomy rather than fully worked philosophical definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian-algebraic style
rubrics_metrics.description: A style centered on Cartesian algebraic methods—mixing algebraic symbolism with geometric ideas (de Lorenzo's list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of a broader listing of historical styles that highlight linguistic/technical shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style of indivisibles
rubrics_metrics.description: A historical style associated with indivisibilist techniques (Cavalieri, early methods antecedent to calculus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Lorenzo lists it; historically contrasted with Archimedean approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational style
rubrics_metrics.description: A style emphasizing operations and algorithmic procedures (one of de Lorenzo's categories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to algorithmic/operational methods in mathematical practice and computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthetic vs analytical styles in geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between synthetic (classical, construction-based) and analytical (coordinate/analytic) approaches in geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: De Lorenzo lists this opposition; historically significant in transitions of methods and presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic style (Indian/Arabic tradition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A style characterized by algorithmic procedures and computational techniques, highlighted as part of historical diversity (Hacking/Corfield mention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hacking and others include the algorithmic style as an addition to Crombie's list; relevant for histories of computation and non-axiomatic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: A style where computation, experimentation, and empirical exploration of examples guide conjecture formation and justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increasingly prominent in modern practice; discussed as methodologically distinct and a promising topic for historiography and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crombie's methodological styles — postulation/axiomatic
rubrics_metrics.description: One of Crombie's listed scientific styles: postulation in the axiomatic mathematical sciences (treating mathematics as postulative systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crombie's list is reproduced/discussed; this item highlights the axiomatic/method-postulation dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crombie's methodological styles — experimental exploration and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Crombie's style emphasizing empirical exploration, measurement, and dealing with complex detectable relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallels in mathematical practice include experimental mathematics and computational exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crombie's methodological styles — hypothetical modelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Crombie's style of using hypothetical models to represent and reason about phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant where modelling and idealization play a central role in mathematical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crombie's methodological styles — ordering by comparison and taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Crombie's style of organizing knowledge by comparison, classification, and taxonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in areas like classification problems (e.g., taxonomy of finite simple groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Crombie's methodological styles — statistical analysis of populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Crombie's style employing statistical methods and population-level analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Less central to pure mathematics but relevant for applied and probabilistic mathematical styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crombie's methodological styles — historical derivation of genetic development
rubrics_metrics.description: Crombie's style that reconstructs genetic or historical development of concepts as a method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful in historical and developmental studies of mathematical concepts and methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs indirect techniques in geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: A contrast between direct constructive techniques (Cavalieri/Torricelli) and indirect (Archimedean-style) methods in geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided as an example of intermediate-level 'styles' that fall between local and methodological categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic vs geometrical approaches in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition observed historically between algebraic methods and geometrical ones in analysis (e.g., Euler vs McLaurin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another example of intermediate styles shaping developments and preferences in mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical vs analytical approaches in complex analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical contrast (Riemann vs Weierstrass) between geometrically-motivated and analytically-rigorous approaches in complex analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates how style affects foundational choices and presentation of theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual vs computational approaches in algebraic number theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between conceptual (abstract) and computational (effective) styles (Dedekind vs Kronecker).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how different priorities (conceptual clarity vs computational effectiveness) constitute distinct styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural vs intuitive styles in algebraic geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between structural/formal approaches (German school) and intuitive/concrete approaches (Italian school) in algebraic geometry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as a case where 'national' or 'school' labels overlap with methodological differences; historians study such cases carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style as non-cognitive 'coloring' (residualist rhetoric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Position that stylistic elements are superficial ornaments of mathematical discourse and do not contribute to cognitive content (Frege-influenced residualist view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dubucs & Dubucs and others frame this as one possible stance in the epistemology of style; treats style as expressive rather than epistemically relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style as epistemically significant (Granger/Hacking views)
rubrics_metrics.description: Position that mathematical style can have cognitive or epistemological roles—affecting what is discovered, how proofs are formed, and the ontology of mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granger offers a systematic theory compatible with mathematical realism; Hacking distinguishes local and methodological styles and explores their epistemological implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granger's program: style as part of scientific practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Granger's systematic effort to analyze 'scientific practice' and argue that style is integral to practice and can carry epistemic import (compatible with realism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granger's work is substantial and argued to have wide philosophical consequences; the SEP entry summarizes rather than fully develops the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bense's 'style as form/aesthetic' view
rubrics_metrics.description: Bense's account treating style as essential form or 'Aesthetic'—connecting histories of art and mathematics while keeping their natures distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bense draws parallels between art-styles and mathematical styles (baroque, romantic), but warns against reducing mathematical style to artistic coincidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bieberbach's racialized/nationalist anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: An historical case where 'style' was used to justify racialized/nationalist claims about mathematical creativity (the 'Deutsche Mathematik' movement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a warning example of misuse: Bieberbach's appropriation of 'style' served ideological ends and involved gerrymandered evidence; modern scholarship rejects such racialized accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical styles as 'intermediate' loci between local and methodological
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal that many mathematical styles occupy an intermediate level — not merely local communities nor wholly methodological lists (examples: Newtonian style, Italian algebraic geometry style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SEP argues the natural locus of mathematical style often falls between Hacking's local and methodological categories; these intermediate styles are characterized by shared methods of enquiry but are not fully universal.
